design_detail: An original laboratory screening study, not a review (the reading list describes it as a review). Liquid from 38 THC-containing cartridges the authors call counterfeit or patient-provided, 4 CBD-containing cartridges and medical-grade cartridges (number not stated; one is described as the reference), obtained from local vape shops and from patients or other people who vaped them, in what the authors call a particular region of New York State, were screened by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) with identification by library match; the liquids of counterfeit and CBD cartridges were screened for 50 elements by ICP-MS; and aerosol from counterfeit cartridges (10 puffs over 10 minutes per cartridge, collected in one-litre vacuum bottles) was sent to a commercial laboratory for volatile-compound analysis by EPA method TO-15 plus library search. The authors hypothesised beforehand that constituents other than vitamin E acetate (VEA) might contribute. Descriptive: no counts per compound, no statistical tests. Version read: the PMC full text of the Toxics article (2020;8(2):25).
can_establish: That a library-matched GC-MS screen of cartridge liquids found hundreds of chemicals (more than 500 across all cartridges), with Table 1 listing 47 entries said to be commonly present in the counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges and not in the others (13 for CBD cartridges, 15 for medical-grade), among them VEA, silicon-containing compounds, terpenes and MCT-type triglycerides; that Table 2 lists 53 volatile compounds for aerosol from counterfeit cartridges (three of them look like laboratory standards), seven on the FDA list of tobacco-smoke constituents; and that silicon, copper, nickel and lead were the most abundant elements in those cartridges' liquid. These are leads for further work.
cannot_establish: Which compounds are truly present (identifications are library matches without reference standards, the method is described as qualitative screening, and some entries look like laboratory standards or reaction products); how often any compound occurred (no counts, and 'commonly present' is not defined; the paper does not say how many of the 38 cartridges held VEA); whether counterfeit cartridges differ from CBD or medical-grade ones in the vapor phase or metals (those were not measured or not shown for the comparison cartridges); how many of the 38 came from patients with EVALI; the exposure a person would receive; or whether any named compound contributes to lung injury.

sample.recruitment: Cartridges were obtained from local vape shops and from individuals or patients (Methods 2.2). The counterfeit brands are said to have been recovered from patients with EVALI and are cited to a published case series (reference 4); hospital staff supplied information on patients' cartridges (Acknowledgments). The paper does not say how many of the 38 came from patients with EVALI and how many from shops or other individuals, when they were collected, or how they were judged counterfeit. Medical-grade cartridges came from a named New York supplier; the number is not stated and the text speaks of one cartridge as the reference.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not described. No manufacturer details were printed on the counterfeit cartridges or packaging. Cannabis oil variants tested were sativa, indica and hybrid.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. The number of cartridges used for vapor-phase analysis and for metals is not stated; the ranges in Table 2 imply at least two cartridges for some compounds.
sample.selection_effects: Convenience samples from one region of New York State (the authors say other regions may differ). The counterfeit group mixes cartridges from patients, individuals and shops. The comparison groups are very small (4 CBD cartridges; medical-grade number not stated) against 38.

exposure.measurement: GC-MS of cartridge rinsates (interior flushed five times with 100 microlitres of methanol) and of neat liquids diluted 100-fold in methanol, mass range 50 to 550, identification by search of the NIST library; no reference standards are described. Vapor phase: aerosol sampled into one-litre vacuum bottles (10 puffs over 10 minutes per cartridge), shipped to a commercial laboratory, analysed by EPA TO-15 for a standard suite of volatile compounds and by library search for 'tentatively identified' compounds; the authors note that any VEA in the aerosol would have condensed on the canister walls before analysis. Elements: ICP-MS with external standards (50 elements at 20 parts per billion). Total volatile organic compounds and particles were measured with a handheld monitor and a particle monitor, described only in the Discussion.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to people. Aerosol was generated at common voltages (3.5 to 5.5 V, per the Discussion) with a device that the Methods do not name; vapor-phase figures are air concentrations in a one-litre canister, which depend on puff volume and dilution that are not given.

comparison.controls: CBD-containing cartridges (4) and medical-grade cartridges (number not stated; a named New York supplier; formulated in coconut oil according to the Discussion). Table 1 lists only compounds 'commonly found' in one category and not in the others, so compounds shared by categories are not shown. Vapor-phase results (Table 2) are for counterfeit cartridges only; metals are reported for counterfeit cartridges only. A separate comparison of total volatile compounds and particles uses pure MCT oil, mineral oil and VEA as the comparators (Discussion).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: How many of the 38 counterfeit cartridges came from patients; the number of cartridges in each analysis; the device used; the age of cartridges and storage before analysis; which chemicals arise from heating, from the device or from preparation in methanol rather than from the liquid.

outcomes.instruments: GC-MS (Agilent 7890A with 5975 detector, NIST library); EPA TO-15 volatile compound analysis by a commercial laboratory; ICP-MS (PerkinElmer NexION 2000); handheld volatile-compound and particle monitors (Discussion only).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors describe the GC-MS method as a preliminary screen with a qualitative result. No reference standards, detection limits, blanks or replicate runs are described for the GC-MS work. Table 2 lists three compounds that are laboratory surrogate or tuning standards of the EPA volatile-compound method (toluene-d8, 1,2-dichloroethane-d4 and bromofluorobenzene, each with a very narrow range) as if they were vapor-phase constituents (editors' note from general analytical chemistry, to be confirmed by a chemist).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Commonly present' is not defined (no number or share of cartridges). Compounds are sorted into groups by the authors' use categories (terpenes, silicon compounds, pesticide constituents, flavour additives, cannabinoids, plasticizers and others, humectants and oils, vitamins, miscellaneous); the same compound (hexadecanoic acid methyl ester) appears under two categories.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes. Table 1 entries (editors' count): 47 for counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges (46 distinct), 13 for CBD, 15 for medical-grade; by category for counterfeit: 13 terpenes, 12 silicon compounds, 7 plasticizers, drugs and manufacturing agents, 3 each flavour additives, cannabinoids and humectants or oils, 2 pesticide constituents (fatty acid methyl esters), 2 vitamins and conjugates (including VEA), 2 miscellaneous. Table 2 (vapor phase of counterfeit cartridges): 53 entries, 51 with concentrations, from 44 to 360,000 micrograms per cubic metre; highest listed ranges for isoprene (8,400 to 360,000), propene (1,500 to 300,000), 2-methylpropene (2,600 to 290,000), acrolein (350 to 150,000) and 1,3-butadiene (98 to 85,000). Metals: silicon, copper, nickel and lead most abundant, very variable between cartridges, up to 600 parts per million (which element is not stated). Total volatile compounds in aerosol, mean with standard error (number of replicates not given): counterfeit cartridges 20.03 (0.59) parts per million against MCT oil 10.33, mineral oil 7.33 and VEA 9.67.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable; the authors state a hypothesis in the Introduction (other constituents may act alone or together with VEA).
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 1 shows only compounds specific to one category, which cannot show what the categories share. Results for metals in CBD cartridges and for the vapor phase of CBD and medical-grade cartridges are not shown although the Methods describe metals screening of CBD liquids and the Conclusion contrasts counterfeit with CBD and medical products. Particle data and the monitors' methods are not given.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A qualitative, library-matched screen listed many compounds in the liquids of 38 counterfeit or patient-provided THC cartridges, including VEA in an unstated number, silicon-containing compounds, terpenes and MCT-type triglycerides; the aerosol of counterfeit cartridges held 51 compounds with listed concentrations, seven of which are on the FDA list of tobacco-smoke constituents; and silicon, copper, nickel and lead were the most abundant elements in their liquid. Comparison cartridges were few (4 CBD; medical-grade number not stated), and neither the vapor phase nor the metals are shown for them.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the study provides additional insights into the chemicals associated with EVALI cartridges and may contribute to the disease mechanism. The conclusion says numerous respiratory toxicants in liquid and vapor phases were not present in the medical or CBD products; that symptoms in EVALI are similar to what can be anticipated from inhaling the compounds detected; and that exposure to a combination of hydrocarbons, oils, other toxic compounds and metals may contribute along with VEA, as opposed to a single cause. Gaps: (1) vapor-phase and metals data are not shown for CBD or medical-grade cartridges, so 'not present' is not tested for them; (2) the list is of library matches with no counts, so presence in any given cartridge is unknown; (3) compound-by-compound toxicity is taken from general toxicology without exposure levels, and the authors themselves say the effect depends on concentration and duration; (4) the symptom match is general; (5) combinations were not tested.

timeline.event: A New York State Department of Health laboratory analysed 38 case-associated fluids with targeted and untargeted methods and found VEA, MCT oil and pesticide residues; it did not report the silicon compounds, hydrocarbons or metals this study highlights.
CDC reported VEA in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients with EVALI and in none of 99 healthy volunteers; its panel was targeted and did not include the compounds this study highlights.

replication.where_it_stands: The presence of VEA and MCT oil in some cartridges is also reported by the other laboratory studies read, with counts; the study's own distinctive claims (silicon compounds, solvent-derived hydrocarbons, metals, vapor-phase toxicants and their role) were not tested by any other source read here. The authors say they are investigating these in models.

funding.funder: This research received no external funding (Funding section).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no actual, potential or perceived competing financial interests (Conflicts of Interest section).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors work at the University of Rochester Medical Center (Environmental Medicine; Pediatric Pulmonology), The College at Brockport, the New York State Department of Health Center for Environmental Health and the University at Buffalo. Universities and a state agency, not the cannabis or tobacco industry; no industry tie is declared.

what_would_settle_it: A repeat with reference standards for each named compound, equal numbers of cartridges of each type with counts per compound reported, the same liquid, aerosol and metals analyses on every type, a named device and defined puffing, provenance recorded (patient, shop, date), and exposure experiments at realistic concentrations to test whether any compound contributes to injury alone or with VEA.

domains.note: 38 counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges from shops, individuals and patients (split not stated), 4 CBD, medical-grade number not stated, vapor-phase and metals numbers not stated; one region.

Library matching without reference standards; described by the authors as qualitative preliminary screening; surrogate standards listed as constituents; some named compounds (acetyl chloride, tetramethyl silicate, 2,2-dimethoxybutane) can react with, or be formed from, methanol, the dilution solvent, so may be preparation artefacts (editors' chemistry note); vapor samples stored and shipped before analysis.

Unequal numbers (38 against 4 and an unstated number); Table 1 lists only compounds exclusive to a category, so longer lists for the larger group are expected; vapor phase and metals not shown for the comparison cartridges.

domains.domain: Separation of findings from inference about cause
domains.note: Compound-by-compound toxicity is inferred from general toxicology (for example 'paralytic agents', silicon dioxide formation) without exposure levels or patient data; the conclusion contrasts counterfeit with medical and CBD products for phases not measured in those products.

No count of cartridges with VEA; compounds named in the text (decane, naphthalene, benzene and aflatoxin B1 in medical-grade cartridges) are absent from the tables or have no method; stated range of 140 to 360,000 against 44 as the lowest in Table 2; methods for volatile-compound and particle monitors missing; one compound in two categories.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a laboratory screening of products (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with domains chosen for product analysis. The overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The paper is open about being a preliminary qualitative screen and that the cause may involve more than VEA, and the hypothesis was stated in advance, but the identifications, counts and comparisons are too incomplete to carry the conclusion about toxicants absent from other products. It may be cited as hypothesis-generating: that a screening of counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges reported chemicals other than VEA, and which kinds. It may not be cited for how many cartridges held any compound, for VEA prevalence, for differences from CBD or medical-grade cartridges in the vapor phase or metals, for the exposure of any person, or for the cause of EVALI.

key_findings.finding: The study screened liquid from 38 cartridges described as counterfeit or patient-provided (THC-containing), 4 CBD-containing cartridges and medical-grade cartridges (number not stated), obtained from local vape shops and from patients or other people who vaped them, in one region of New York State, to test the hypothesis that constituents other than VEA, alone or with VEA, might injure the lung. It is a laboratory study, not a review.

More than 500 chemicals were found across the tested cartridges, mostly terpenes and silicon compounds. Chemicals described as specific to the counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges include 2,2-dimethoxybutane, tetramethyl silicate, methyl and ethyl esters, siloxanes, acetates including VEA, benzophenone, glycerol tricaprylate and THC derivatives. Table 1 lists 47 entries for these cartridges, 13 for CBD and 15 for medical-grade (editors' count). No count of cartridges containing VEA is given.

Vapor phase of counterfeit cartridges: over 50 chemicals with concentrations listed (Table 2 has 53 entries, 51 with concentrations, 44 to 360,000 micrograms per cubic metre), mostly volatile hydrocarbons and solvents; seven are on the FDA list of harmful or potentially harmful constituents of tobacco products and smoke (isoprene, acetaldehyde, ethylbenzene, toluene, acrolein, 1,3-butadiene, benzene). VEA was not found in the vapor phase, which the authors suggest may be due to condensation before analysis.

Elements in the liquid of counterfeit patient cartridges: silicon, copper, nickel and lead were the most abundant, very variable between cartridges, up to 600 parts per million. The Methods say CBD cartridges' liquids were screened too; no results are given for them.

The authors say they detected VEA in many EVALI-associated liquids but not in all, and that this does not mean the other cartridges patients used earlier lacked it, since only what was provided was tested. Medical-grade cartridges held retinol (vitamin A) acetate rather than VEA, and fewer contaminants than counterfeit cartridges, though some harmful chemicals were still identified in them.

Total volatile compounds in aerosol were higher from counterfeit patient cartridges (20.03, standard error 0.59, parts per million) than from MCT oil (10.33), mineral oil (7.33) or VEA (9.67), and particle concentrations were also higher; the comparators are pure oils, the numbers of replicates are not given and the monitors are not described in the Methods.

Stated limits: the GC-MS method was a preliminary screen and the findings are qualitative; samples came from one region of New York State; the effect of any constituent depends on concentration and duration; susceptibility factors and use of other vaping products may contribute because not all people who used THC cartridges were hospitalised; legal restrictions limit toxicology research on cannabis products.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph (concentration and duration) and 10th and 11th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Context quoted from other sources (second-hand): over 2,500 hospitalised patients by December 2019, most men younger than 35; most patients report vaping THC-containing counterfeit street products; VEA is described as a key agent, though inhaled VEA is not a proven cause of lung damage, and animal studies cited by the authors suggest VEA may protect against effects of cigarette smoke and bacterial toxin; a cited study found no VEA in licit UK e-cigarette products; EVALI has been seen almost only in North America.
key_findings.note: None of the cited sources was read for this card.

key_findings.finding: Conclusion as written: numerous respiratory toxicants in liquid and vapor phases were not present in the medical or CBD vape products; a combination of hydrocarbons, oils, other toxic compounds and metals may contribute to EVALI together with VEA rather than a single agent; the authors are investigating this in models.

Funding: none external. Declared conflicts: none. Authors are at the University of Rochester Medical Center, The College at Brockport, the New York State Department of Health Center for Environmental Health and the University at Buffalo.
key_findings.locator: Funding; Conflicts of Interest; author affiliations

reporting_issues.issue: The paper says VEA was in many but not all counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges and gives no count; the share of the 38 containing VEA, MCT oil or any other named compound is not reported anywhere.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results 3.1; Discussion, 6th paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The study cannot be cited for how common VEA or any other compound was; for VEA prevalence a counted source (duffy_2020) is needed.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 lists toluene-d8, 1,2-dichloroethane-d4 and bromofluorobenzene as vapor-phase constituents, each with a very narrow range (510 to 516, 391 to 395 and 556 to 561 micrograms per cubic metre). These are deuterated or halogenated compounds that the EPA volatile-compound method uses as laboratory surrogate or tuning standards, and a deuterated compound is not expected in a cartridge.
reporting_issues.consequence: The count of over 50 vapor-phase chemicals may include laboratory standards (editors' note from general analytical chemistry, to be confirmed by a chemist); the true count would be 50 or fewer.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the vapor-phase range as 140 to 360,000 micrograms per cubic metre; Table 2 lists lower values (n-hexane from 44, 2-butanone from 94, benzene from 97, 1,3-butadiene from 98).
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated range does not match the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion says respiratory toxicants in both phases were not present in the medical or CBD products. Vapor-phase results (Table 2) are for counterfeit cartridges only, and metals results are for counterfeit cartridges only.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results 3.2 and 3.3; Discussion, 12th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: For the vapor phase and metals the claimed contrast has no data shown for the comparison products.

reporting_issues.issue: Compounds named in the text as found are not in the tables or have no method: decane and naphthalene (the Conclusion calls them semi-volatile hydrocarbons; Table 1 lists undecane and no naphthalene), and benzene and aflatoxin B1 in medical-grade cartridges (benzene is in Table 2 for counterfeit cartridges only; the Methods describe no test for aflatoxin).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results 3.1; Discussion, 3rd, 6th and 7th paragraphs; Tables 1 and 2
reporting_issues.consequence: These specific claims cannot be checked from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Hexadecanoic acid methyl ester is listed for counterfeit cartridges both as a pesticide constituent and as a plasticizer or manufacturing agent; fatty acid methyl esters are the only 'pesticide constituents' listed, and no targeted pesticide analysis was done.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pesticide finding here is a category label from a library match; targeted pesticide measurements are in duffy_2020.

reporting_issues.issue: Methods for the volatile-compound monitor and the particle monitor, the device and its settings, the number of cartridges in the vapor-phase and metals work, and the replicate numbers behind the means with standard errors are not given.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods 2.4 and 2.5; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The aerosol comparisons cannot be reproduced or weighed.

reporting_issues.issue: The reading list describes this paper as a review; it is an original laboratory study.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is treated here as primary (low-grade) laboratory evidence, not as a summary of other work.
